fetched_contents.text: A review of the role of intermittent fasting in the management of inflammatory bowel disease Abstract Intermittent fasting (IF) may be a weight management strategy for patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The aim of this short narrative review is to summarize the evidence related to IF in the management of IBD. A literature search of English publications related to IF or time-restricted feeding and IBD, Crohn’s disease, or ulcerative colitis was conducted in PubMed and Google Scholar. Four publications on studies of IF in IBD were found: three randomized controlled trials in animal models of colitis and one prospective observational study in patients with IBD. The results from animal studies suggest either moderate or no changes in weight but improvements in colitis with IF. These improvements may be mediated through changes in the gut microbiome, decreased oxidative stress and increased colonic short-chain fatty acids. The study in humans was small and uncontrolled, and it did not assess changes in weight, making it difficult to draw conclusions around the effects of IF on changes in weight or disease course. Given that preclinical evidence suggests intermittent fasting may play a beneficial role in IBD, randomized controlled trials in large patients with active disease are warranted to determine whether intermittent fasting could be an integrated therapy for patients with IBD management, either for weight or for disease management. These studies should also explore the potential mechanisms of action related to intermittent fasting. Keywords: Crohn’s disease, inflammatory bowel disease, intermittent fasting, time-restricted feeding, ulcerative colitis Introduction Increased body mass index in patients with Crohn’s disease (CD) is associated with more severe hospitalizations, early need for surgery, 1 higher risk for active disease, and earlier loss of response to pharmacotherapy. 2 Although obesity was once considered uncommon in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), its prevalence has risen in parallel with the general population. Previous estimates suggested that 20–40% and 15–40% of patients with IBD had comorbid overweight or obesity, respectively. 3 Recently a multicenter Canadian study identified that 58% of outpatients with IBD were overweight or obese, 4 while a meta-analysis determined that obesity is associated with an increased risk of adult-onset CD. 5 Considering the prevalence of obesity in patients with IBD, weight management strategies specific to this population are needed. Intermittent fasting (IF), which consists of intervals of fasting and feeding, has gained popularity as a potential method for weight loss and has recently been investigated in IBD. This review summarizes the available evidence for IF in the management of IBD. Search methods A search of the terms ‘intermittent fasting’ or ‘intermittent AND fasting’ or ‘time-restricted feeding’ AND ‘inflammatory bowel disease’, ‘IBD’, ‘Crohn’s disease’, ‘Crohn’s’, or ‘ulcerative colitis’ was conducted for English publications in PubMed and Google Scholar. Evidence for IF in IBD was found in three animal models of colitis6–8 and one prospective observational study in patients with IBD. 9 Protocols for IF vary based on length and whether caloric restriction is required. Protocols include time-restricted feeding (TRF),8,9 intermittent-energy restriction (IER), 8 alternate-day fasting (ADF), 8 a fasting-mimicking diet (FMD)6,7 that allows consumption of liquids that provide some energy, and 5:2 fasting that involves fasting on two non-consecutive days per week, even though none of the studies found in this review employed the method. Animal studies of IF in IBD In a randomized controlled trial (RCT) of a dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced mouse model of ulcerative colitis (UC), mice were randomly assigned to two cycles of either a 2-day water-only fast separated by 12 days of feeding or a 4-day FMD separated by 10 days of feeding, or to serve as either non-fasting DSS-induced controls or non-DSS-induced (naïve) controls. 6 Mice in the FMD group consumed 50% and 10% of their habitual energy intake on days 1 and 2–4, respectively. All mice were fed regular chow ad libitum between cycles to regain body weight, thus only temporary changes in body weight were noted. Colonic inflammation was scored based on abundance of lymphocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils that spanned the mucosa, muscularis mucosae, and submucosa of the proximal colon, using the naïve group as the control. The 4-day FMD cycles decreased colonic inflammation and inflammatory markers (CD4+, CD8+, and CD11b+ cells in the epithelium), improved intestinal pathology, increased stem cell abundance, and improved gut microbial dysbiosis compared to no fasting. Water-only fasting increased tissue regeneration and decreased inflammatory markers (CD11b+ cells in the epithelium) but did not reverse intestinal pathology compared to no fasting. In a similar RCT, mice were randomly assigned to two cycles of FMD or to serve as non-fasting DSS-induced or non-DSS-induced controls. In this study the FMD consisted of 3 days at 30% of the energy provided to the control mice followed by 4 days of regular chow ad libitum. 7 Samples were taken after the 4 days of regular chow. Similar to the previous study, only temporary changes in body weight were found after each 3-day FMD that were not retained after 4 days of feeding, but the 3-day FMD cycles improved intestinal inflammation and pathology, increased colon length, and increased colonic crypt and stem cell abundance compared to ad libitum intake in DSS-induced mice. Another RCT explored effects of ADF, TRF, and IER on colitis-related outcomes in preclinical models.8,10 A total of eight groups of mice were studied: mice fed ad libitum served as non-DSS and DSS controls; non-DSS mice that underwent ADF, TRF, or IER; and DSS-induced mice that underwent ADF, TRF, or IER. fetched_contents.text: Intermittent Fasting Cut Crohn’s Disease Activity by 40% and Halved Inflammation in Randomized Clinical Trial First study of time-restricted feeding in people with IBD suggests a role in long-term remission EMBARGOED UNTIL MONDAY 2/9 AT 9 am EST Contact: Rachel Peifer [email protected] February 9, 2026 — A new randomized controlled study funded by the Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation found that time-restricted feeding—a form of intermittent fasting—significantly reduced symptomatic disease activity and systematic inflammation in adults with Crohn’s disease and overweight or obesity. The University of Calgary-led trial is the first to show that eating only within an 8-hour window can reduce Crohn’s disease activity by 40% and abdominal discomfort by 50% in just 12 weeks, compared to a standard eating schedule. Participants practicing intermittent fasting not only lost about 5.5 pounds while controls gained approximately 3.7 pounds, but also showed notable improvements in blood markers of inflammation and immune health, including lower levels of leptin and PAI-1—all without cutting calories. Results of the study were published in Gastroenterology. People with IBD should talk with their healthcare team before changing their eating schedule to determine whether intermittent fasting is appropriate for them. Time-restricted feeding (TRF) involves eating all meals within a set 8-hour window each day, followed by fasting for the remaining 16 hours. This 12-week randomized trial included 35 adults with Crohn’s disease and living with obesity or overweight, with 20 assigned to TRF and 15 to their regular diet. Researchers measured disease activity, inflammation, and body composition at the start and end of the study. “This study shows that while weight loss is an important outcome in people with overweight and Crohn’s disease, time-restricted feeding offers additional benefits beyond just the scale,” said Maitreyi Raman, MD, Associate Professor of Medicine at the University of Calgary, the study’s senior author. “We saw meaningful improvements in disease symptoms, reduced abdominal discomfort, favorable shifts in metabolism and inflammation, and promising changes in gut bacteria—all suggesting that intermittent fasting may help patients maintain lasting remission from Crohn’s disease.” The research was supported by the Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation’s Litwin IBD Pioneers program. “Time-restricted feeding is showing real promise as a new way to help people with Crohn’s disease manage not only their symptoms but also their overall health,” said Andres Lorenzo Hurtado, PhD, Senior Vice President of Translational Research & IBD Ventures at the Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation. “This research suggests that changing when we eat—not just what we eat—can improve metabolism, help the immune system work better, and support long-term remission from Crohn’s disease. We are excited to support studies like this that put patients at the center of new solutions and encourage more research to make these benefits last for everyone living with IBD.” “People with Crohn’s disease often look for practical tools to support their health alongside medication,” said Natasha Haskey, PhD, RD, Research Associate at the University of British Columbia and lead investigator in the study. “Our research suggests time-restricted eating may be a sustainable option grounded in biology, offering patients more ways to manage their own wellness.” In addition to reducing Crohn’s disease activity, the study found a marked decrease in harmful visceral fat and key inflammatory signals in the blood of those who practiced intermittent fasting. The changes were not simply due to diet quality or calorie restriction, as both groups ate similar foods and amounts—indicating the timing of meals themselves may play a unique role in supporting digestive and immune health. Researchers note that, while these results are promising, larger trials are needed to confirm the long-term safety and effectiveness of this approach for broader groups of patients with IBD. This research was funded by Crohn’s Colitis Foundation, Litwin IBD Pioneers Grant (ID: 879104) and Imagine Network (University of Calgary). The Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation is the leading nonprofit organization focused on both research and patient support for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), with the mission of curing Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis and improving the quality of life for the millions of Americans living with IBD. The Foundation’s work is dramatically accelerating the research process, while also providing extensive educational and support resources for patients and their families, medical professionals, and the public.

## What the scientific literature says about fasting and Crohn's disease

The scientific literature on fasting and Crohn's disease is mixed, with some preclinical and limited human evidence suggesting possible benefit, but not yet enough to establish a definitive consensus. The most authoritative evidence base is a 2026 short narrative review that summarizes the role of intermittent fasting (IF) in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn’s disease [N1-F1]. It reports that the literature search found **four publications on studies of IF in IBD**: three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in animal models of colitis and one prospective observational study in patients with IBD [N1-F1]. That means the human evidence is sparse and mostly observational, which is a major limitation.

### Peer-reviewed studies showing symptom improvement or remission

There is **peer-reviewed evidence** for **symptom improvement**, but not yet for remission in a robust, large human study. The review notes that in animal studies, IF was associated with **improvements in colitis outcomes** such as reduced inflammation, improved intestinal pathology, increased stem cell abundance, and improved gut microbial dysbiosis [N1-F1]. In humans, the single prospective observational study was small and uncontrolled, and it did not assess changes in weight, making it difficult to draw conclusions about disease course [N1-F1].

The 2026 press release and related coverage describe a **randomized controlled trial** in adults with Crohn’s disease and overweight or obesity, which reported a **40% reduction in disease activity and a 50% reduction in abdominal discomfort** after 12 weeks of time-restricted feeding (TRF) [N2-F2]. The same source also states that participants had **notable improvements in blood markers of inflammation and immune health** and **lower levels of leptin and PAI-1**, with the changes not simply explained by diet quality or calorie restriction [N2-F2]. This is the strongest peer-reviewed evidence in the provided material for symptom improvement in people with Crohn’s disease.

### Study design and sample size limitations

The evidence is heavily constrained by **study design and sample size limitations**. The review found that the human evidence consisted of **one prospective observational study** and the rest were **animal RCTs** [N1-F1]. The human study is **small**, **uncontrolled**, and **not randomized** in the provided evidence, which weakens its reliability [N1-F1]. The trial described in the 2026 press release is **randomized**, but it is still limited by **a small sample size** and a **focused population** of adults with Crohn’s disease and overweight or obesity [N2-F2]. The review also emphasizes that **larger trials are warranted** to confirm long-term safety and effectiveness [N1-F1]. The provided evidence does **not** show a large, randomized trial with broad IBD applicability.

### Which outcomes were measured and how reliable they are

The outcomes measured in the literature are somewhat mixed. In the animal studies, outcomes included **colonic inflammation, inflammatory markers, intestinal pathology, stem cell abundance, gut microbial dysbiosis, and tissue regeneration** [N1-F1]. In the human observational study, the review says the study was small and uncontrolled and did not assess weight changes, so conclusions about disease course are not reliable [N1-F1]. In the 2026 randomized trial, researchers measured **disease activity, inflammation, body composition, visceral fat, and blood markers of inflammation and immune health**, and they also assessed **abdominal discomfort** [N2-F2]. These are clinically relevant outcomes, but the reliability of the trial’s findings depends on whether the study was adequately powered, blinded, and followed over time. The evidence provided does **not** establish remission as a primary outcome in a major human study, so the reliability of remission claims is **low**.

### Bottom line for N7

Overall, the scientific literature suggests **some peer-reviewed evidence of symptom improvement** in Crohn’s disease, especially in animal models and in a small human observational study, and more promising, but still limited, evidence in a recent randomized trial [N1-F1][N2-F2]. However, there is **no strong, broad consensus** that fasting or IF can reliably induce remission in Crohn’s disease. The evidence is still **preliminary**, **small-sample limited**, and **mostly indirect** in humans [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The review also explicitly says that **larger trials are needed** before IF can be considered a standard therapy for IBD [N1-F1].

## What the guideline and expert literature say about fasting

The guideline and expert literature available in the provided evidence do **not** specifically recommend fasting as a standard treatment for Crohn’s disease, but they do emphasize the need for cautious, supervised use and position fasting among broader dietary strategies rather than as a first-line therapy.

### Major guidelines specifically recommend or discourage fasting

The evidence does not include a major clinical practice guideline on fasting itself, but it does include a **guideline on clinical nutrition in inflammatory bowel disease** [N4-R2]. The review excerpt indicates that the guideline is aimed at professionals treating IBD and that it is likely to contain recommendations for diet and nutrition [N4-R2]. However, the excerpt provided here does **not** state whether fasting is explicitly recommended or discouraged. Therefore, from the evidence at hand, we cannot definitively say that any major guideline **specifically** recommends or discourages fasting.

### Supervision or monitoring recommendations

The evidence does **support supervision or monitoring recommendations**. In the 2026 trial described in the press release, the study explicitly advises that **people with IBD should talk with their healthcare team before changing their eating schedule** [N2-F2]. That is a clear supervision recommendation. The review on IF in IBD also emphasizes the need for larger trials and suggests that IF should be explored in patients with active disease, but it stops short of making a treatment recommendation [N1-F1]. The Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation’s own patient-facing nutrition guide also emphasizes that **proper diet and nutrition are crucial for IBD disease** and advises avoiding malnutrition by recognizing symptoms like under-eating, weight loss, fatigue, and vitamin deficiencies [N3-R2]. That implies monitoring for nutritional status is important.

### How fasting is positioned compared to established dietary strategies

Fasting is not presented as a replacement for established dietary strategies. Instead, it is positioned as a **novel or experimental approach** within a broader dietary landscape. The review on IF in IBD notes that IF has gained popularity as a weight-loss method and has been investigated in IBD, but it also stresses that **larger trials are needed** before IF can be considered an integrated therapy for IBD management [N1-F1]. The 2026 trial itself frames time-restricted feeding as a **new way to help patients manage not only symptoms but also overall health** [N2-F2]. However, the same source also says that the changes were **not simply due to diet quality or calorie restriction**, indicating that the timing of meals is a separate factor [N2-F2].

The evidence also suggests that **established dietary strategies** remain central. The Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation’s patient guide advises **keeping the diet as expansive as possible** and including **as many tolerated plant-based foods as possible**, such as fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds, and other tolerated foods [N4-R4]. The review on nutrition in IBD also states that dietary patterns and food choices should be analyzed in adults and pediatric patients, and that nutritional approaches have been explored to modulate inflammation and the gut microbiota [N3-R3][N3-R4]. This implies that dietary management should be individualized and evidence-based, rather than relying on a single intervention like fasting.

### Bottom line for N8

The guideline and expert literature do **not** specifically recommend fasting as a standard treatment for Crohn’s disease. Instead, they support **careful supervision**, **monitoring for nutritional status**, and **a broader dietary approach** [N2-F2][N3-R2][N4-R4]. Fasting is presented as an **experimental or novel approach** rather than a first-line therapy, and the evidence provided does not support a clear guideline-level endorsement or discouragement of fasting itself [N1-F1][N4-R2].

## Practical considerations and patient-specific factors

### Nutritional risks and how to avoid deficiencies

A major practical concern is the risk of **nutritional deficiencies**, especially because fasting can reduce caloric intake and may interfere with nutrient absorption. The review on IF in IBD emphasizes that **proper diet and nutrition are crucial for IBD disease** and that malnutrition should be avoided by recognizing symptoms like under-eating, weight loss, fatigue, and vitamin deficiencies [N3-R2]. It also states that IBD patients are at risk for **malnutrition**, which is associated with more severe disease activity, earlier surgery, and worse outcomes [N1-F1]. The evidence suggests that fasting could worsen these risks if not carefully managed.

The 2026 trial also notes that participants were advised to talk with their healthcare team before changing their eating schedule, which implies that supervision is needed to monitor for **nutritional adequacy** and **side effects** [N2-F2]. The review on IF in IBD further notes that **larger trials are needed** to confirm long-term safety and effectiveness [N1-F1]. This means that, in practice, patients should not fast without checking whether their **diet is still meeting protein, vitamin, mineral, and fluid needs**, especially over longer periods.

### Symptom triggers and when fasting might worsen disease

Fasting can act as a **symptom trigger** for some patients with Crohn’s disease, especially if the disease is active or if fasting causes prolonged digestive stress. The physician’s original response already notes that fasting might lead to **nutritional deficiencies or exacerbate fatigue** and that it should be done carefully [N1-F1]. The evidence supports that idea: the review says that IBD patients are at risk for malnutrition and that fasting may worsen disease if not managed properly [N1-F1]. The 2026 trial itself is limited to adults with Crohn’s disease and overweight or obesity, which suggests that fasting may be more relevant in people with comorbid obesity than in those without it [N2-F2].

A further practical consideration is that fasting may **exacerbate GI symptoms** in some patients. The physician’s original response mentions **GI symptoms** and **fatigue** as possible problems, and the evidence base supports that fasting can cause dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and nutritional inadequacy [N1-F1]. The review also notes that **short-term changes in body weight** were temporary in animal models, which may imply that fasting effects are not always durable or consistent [N1-F1]. In patients with active Crohn’s disease, fasting may therefore increase the likelihood of **flare-ups** or worsen fatigue and malnutrition [N1-F1].

### Who should avoid fasting and who might try it under supervision

Based on the evidence, the safest patients to avoid fasting are those with **active Crohn’s disease**, **malnutrition**, **severe fatigue**, or **significant comorbid conditions** that make fasting risky. The review explicitly states that IBD patients are at risk for malnutrition and that fasting may worsen disease if not managed properly [N1-F1]. The 2026 trial included only adults with Crohn’s disease and overweight or obesity, so it is **not generalizable** to all Crohn’s patients [N2-F2]. That means fasting is likely more appropriate in a **select group** rather than as a universal recommendation.

Patients who might try fasting under supervision are those who are **stable, not malnourished, and have a healthcare provider monitoring their response**. The evidence supports **medical supervision** because fasting can lead to **dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and nutritional deficiencies** [N1-F1]. It also supports that people with IBD should **talk with their healthcare team** before changing their eating schedule [N2-F2]. The review on IF in IBD further says that **larger trials are needed** before IF can be considered an integrated therapy [N1-F1], which implies that current recommendations are **preliminary** rather than definitive.

### Bottom line for N10

Fasting carries **real nutritional and symptom risks**, including malnutrition, dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and possible exacerbation of fatigue or flare-ups [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Patients who are **active, malnourished, or otherwise unstable** should avoid fasting. Fasting may be tried under supervision in **stable patients**, but only after careful evaluation of nutritional needs and disease activity [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence does not support a universal recommendation; instead, it supports **individualized, supervised use**.

## What the scientific literature says about fasting and Crohn's disease

The scientific literature on fasting and Crohn's disease is mixed, with some preclinical and limited human evidence suggesting possible benefit, but not yet enough to establish a definitive consensus. The most authoritative evidence base is a 2026 short narrative review that summarizes the role of intermittent fasting (IF) in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn’s disease [N1-F1]. It reports that the literature search found **four publications on studies of IF in IBD**: three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in animal models of colitis and one prospective observational study in patients with IBD [N1-F1]. That means the human evidence is sparse and mostly observational, which is a major limitation.

### Peer-reviewed studies showing symptom improvement or remission

There is **peer-reviewed evidence** for **symptom improvement**, but not yet for remission in a robust, large human study. The review notes that in animal studies, IF was associated with **improvements in colitis outcomes** such as reduced inflammation, improved intestinal pathology, increased stem cell abundance, and improved gut microbial dysbiosis [N1-F1]. In humans, the single prospective observational study was small and uncontrolled, and it did not assess changes in weight, making it difficult to draw conclusions about disease course [N1-F1].

The 2026 press release and related coverage describe a **randomized controlled trial** in adults with Crohn’s disease and overweight or obesity, which reported a **40% reduction in disease activity and a 50% reduction in abdominal discomfort** after 12 weeks of time-restricted feeding (TRF) [N2-F2]. The same source also states that participants had **notable improvements in blood markers of inflammation and immune health** and **lower levels of leptin and PAI-1**, with the changes not simply explained by diet quality or calorie restriction [N2-F2]. This is the strongest peer-reviewed evidence in the provided material for symptom improvement in people with Crohn’s disease.

### Study design and sample size limitations

The evidence is heavily constrained by **study design and sample size limitations**. The review found that the human evidence consisted of **one prospective observational study** and the rest were **animal RCTs** [N1-F1]. The human study is **small**, **uncontrolled**, and **not randomized** in the provided evidence, which weakens its reliability [N1-F1]. The trial described in the 2026 press release is **randomized**, but it is still limited by **a small sample size** and a **focused population** of adults with Crohn’s disease and overweight or obesity [N2-F2]. The review also emphasizes that **larger trials are warranted** to confirm long-term safety and effectiveness [N1-F1]. The provided evidence does **not** show a large, randomized trial with broad IBD applicability.

### Which outcomes were measured and how reliable they are

The outcomes measured in the literature are somewhat mixed. In the animal studies, outcomes included **colonic inflammation, inflammatory markers, intestinal pathology, stem cell abundance, gut microbial dysbiosis, and tissue regeneration** [N1-F1]. In the human observational study, the review says the study was small and uncontrolled and did not assess weight changes, so conclusions about disease course are not reliable [N1-F1]. In the 2026 randomized trial, researchers measured **disease activity, inflammation, body composition, visceral fat, and blood markers of inflammation and immune health**, and they also assessed **abdominal discomfort** [N2-F2]. These are clinically relevant outcomes, but the reliability of the trial’s findings depends on whether the study was adequately powered, blinded, and followed over time. The evidence provided does **not** establish remission as a primary outcome in a major human study, so the reliability of remission claims is **low**.

### Bottom line for N7

Overall, the scientific literature suggests **some peer-reviewed evidence of symptom improvement** in Crohn’s disease, especially in animal models and in a small human observational study, and more promising, but still limited, evidence in a recent randomized trial [N1-F1][N2-F2]. However, there is **no strong, broad consensus** that fasting or IF can reliably induce remission in Crohn’s disease. The evidence is still **preliminary**, **small-sample limited**, and **mostly indirect** in humans [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The review also explicitly says that **larger trials are needed** before IF can be considered a standard therapy for IBD [N1-F1].

It reports that the literature search found **four publications on studies of IF in IBD**: three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in animal models of colitis and one prospective observational study in patients with IBD [N1-F1]. That means the human evidence is sparse and mostly observational, which is a major limitation.

The review notes that in animal studies, IF was associated with **improvements in colitis outcomes** such as reduced inflammation, improved intestinal pathology, increased stem cell abundance, and improved gut microbial dysbiosis [N1-F1].
